subject: physics
title: Damping, forced oscillations and resonance
key_idea: Damping takes energy from an oscillator, so its amplitude falls. A system driven at its natural frequency absorbs energy most efficiently, and its amplitude becomes very large. This is resonance.

blocks.text: This section separates an oscillator left alone from one that is pushed by an outside source.

items.meaning: An oscillation at the natural frequency, with no repeating external force acting after the start.
The frequency at which a system oscillates freely after being disturbed.
An oscillation caused by a periodic external force, called the driving force.
The frequency of the external force acting on the system.

items: A free oscillator, once set going, oscillates at its natural frequency. Its energy stays constant if there is no damping.
A forced oscillator is made to oscillate at the **driving frequency**, not at its natural frequency.
At first the motion is irregular. After a short time it settles at the driving frequency.
The amplitude of a forced oscillation depends on how close the driving frequency is to the natural frequency.
Free: oscillates at its natural frequency.
Forced: oscillates at the driving frequency.
The amplitude depends on how close the two frequencies are.

blocks.text: Damping happens when a resistive force acts on an oscillating system.

items: Air resistance, friction and viscous drag do work against the motion.
Energy is transferred from the oscillator to the surroundings, mostly as thermal energy.
The amplitude falls with each cycle. The period is almost unchanged for light damping.
The more damping, the faster the amplitude decays.

columns: What happens after a displacement and release
rows: Oscillates with the amplitude decreasing gradually.
Returns to equilibrium in the shortest time, without oscillating.
Returns to equilibrium very slowly, without oscillating.

items: Car suspensions and door closers are designed with close to critical damping.
Plastic deformation of a ductile material takes energy out of an oscillation. The material permanently changes shape, and the work done does not return as elastic energy.
A resistive force removes energy and the amplitude falls.
Light damping oscillates, critical damping returns fastest, heavy damping returns slowly.

blocks.text: Resonance is the large-amplitude oscillation produced when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency.

items: At resonance the driving force is in step with the motion (a quarter of a cycle ahead of the displacement).
The driver then does positive work on the system in every cycle, so energy transfers to it as efficiently as possible.
The amplitude rises until the energy lost to damping per cycle equals the energy supplied.
With no damping at all, the amplitude at resonance would grow without limit.

diagram.alt: Amplitude against driving frequency for a lightly damped and a heavily damped system. The light damping curve has a tall, sharp peak at the natural frequency. The heavy damping curve has a low, broad peak, slightly below the natural frequency.

x.label: Driving frequency as a multiple of the natural frequency

items: At low driving frequency the amplitude is small, and the system moves with the driver.
The peak is at, or just below, the natural frequency.
More damping lowers the peak and makes it **less sharp**, so the curve is wider.
Well above the natural frequency the amplitude is small again.
Resonance: maximum amplitude when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.
Damping reduces the peak amplitude and makes the peak less sharp.

blocks.text: Resonance can be useful or harmful, depending on the situation.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Examples of resonance are sorted into those that are useful and those that are a problem.
diagram.prompt: Sort each example by whether resonance is useful or a problem.

items.text: Tuning a radio to a station
A musical instrument's air column or strings producing a loud note
A bridge shaken by wind or marching feet
A building shaken by an earthquake
A loose panel rattling on a car at a certain engine speed
A glass shattering when a singer holds its note

items: In a stationary wave, an air column or a string resonates when the driving frequency matches one of its natural frequencies.
Damping is added to reduce harmful resonance: shock absorbers, tuned mass dampers in tall buildings, and flexible foundations.
Resonance helps in tuning, instruments and scanners.
It harms bridges, buildings and machines unless damping is added.

checks.q: State what is meant by resonance.
checks.a: The amplitude of a forced oscillation is a maximum when the driving frequency is equal to the natural frequency of the system.

checks.q: Explain the effect of increasing the damping on the resonance curve of a system.
checks.a: The peak amplitude is lower, the peak is broader (less sharp), and the peak frequency moves slightly below the natural frequency.

checks.q: Describe, in terms of energy, why the amplitude of a freely oscillating pendulum falls with time.
checks.a: Air resistance (a resistive force) does work against the motion. Energy is transferred from the pendulum to the surroundings, so its total energy and amplitude decrease.

items: The treatment is qualitative: describe free and forced vibrations, and no calculations are needed.
Explain resonance and the effects of damping on the sharpness of resonance.
Use examples in mechanical systems and in stationary waves, such as a string or an air column.
Describe how the amplitude of a forced oscillation changes at and around the natural frequency: it increases as the driving frequency approaches it, peaks at resonance, then falls.
Say qualitatively how damping affects resonance: lower and broader peak.
Explain how plastic deformation of ductile materials reduces amplitude: as the material is stretched past its elastic limit, work is done permanently deforming it, so energy is dissipated each cycle.
Ductile materials, such as copper or mild steel, are used in structures to absorb energy from vibrations.

blocks.text: You must be able to sketch displacement–time graphs for the three types of damping.

items: **Light:** a sine-like wave inside a decaying envelope. The peaks fall exponentially and the period stays almost constant.
**Critical:** the displacement falls to zero in the shortest time and does not pass through zero. There is no oscillation.
**Heavy:** the displacement falls to zero more slowly than for critical damping, with no oscillation.
Start each sketch from the same positive displacement at t = 0.
A common setup is a mass on a spring driven by a vibration generator, or a Barton's pendulum.
Vary the driving frequency in steps, and measure the amplitude at each. Plot amplitude against driving frequency.
Wait until the amplitude settles at each frequency before measuring.
Add card to the mass to increase damping, and repeat. The peak is lower and broader.
Other systems to observe: a pendulum, a flexible ruler clamped at one end, and a metal sheet or glass with a loudspeaker.
